title: Illumiware: Painting with Light’s vision for more adaptable attractions
summary:
Across the attractions industry, operators are seeking ways to refresh environments, give guests new reasons to visit, and make existing spaces more adaptable.

For many, however, changing the guest experience still requires significant investment in physical theming and temporary installations. This can be particularly challenging for seasonal events, where spaces may need to be transformed several times a year.

Belgian creative design firm Painting with Light has developed Illumiware in response, drawing on its experience in lighting, video and immersive design.

The new product brand focuses on making the visual technologies used in immersive environments more accessible, with a range of robust, standardised hardware designed to work with changing digital content.


This approach lets operators use the same physical infrastructure for different experiences and events, rather than requiring a new installation for each one.

Illumiware will make its global debut at IAAPA Expo Europe, where it will showcase the IllumiSphere, a 360-degree holographic LED display, alongside the IllumiTree, a 3.5-metre-tall visual installation. Both combine digital content with physical environments, offering attractions new ways to change a space without completely reworking it.

​From lighting design to digital environments


Illumiware builds on Painting with Light’s experience in lighting, video and immersive design. Founder and CEO Luc Peumans has seen display technology develop significantly over his career, bringing new creative possibilities to attractions and other entertainment environments.


He sees the growth of LED technology as particularly significant. Higher-resolution displays and increasingly sophisticated content let designers create more realistic, flexible environments, while improvements in reliability and affordability are making the technology more accessible.

“The quality [of LED screens] has improved so much that it gives so many possibilities,” Peumans says. “The content you can create becomes so realistic.”

For Peumans, the potential goes beyond standalone displays. He sees digital surfaces becoming an increasingly integrated part of location-based entertainment, allowing operators to change a space's look and atmosphere without physically altering it.

“I believe that in the future all wallpaper will be replaced by LED screens,” he says. “With this trend, you can change atmospheres very drastically. It allows you, with the press of a button, to go from atmosphere one to atmosphere two.”

This could be particularly relevant to venues that need to refresh their environments throughout the year. Seasonal changes traditionally involve physical decorations, installations and associated labour. Digital content offers an alternative, allowing the same infrastructure to support different themes and occasions.

“A lot of operators are looking for solutions where they have year-long access to create different atmospheres so that people come back again,” Peumans says.

​Designing technology around the story


Painting with Light has already explored the potential of flexible digital scenery through projects including the Plopsa Theatre, where the company designed and delivered a moving LED screen installation covering around 275 square metres.

The system allows the venue to create different scenic environments using the same physical infrastructure. Shows can therefore be changed without rebuilding the stage, giving the operator greater flexibility.

“With moving LED walls, you can make such realistic sceneries that people are blown away, but you can do two different kinds of shows very easily,” Peumans says. “Today you play this show, tomorrow you play another, and with minimal effort you can make it change.”


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by PWL - Painting With Light (@pwl_be)

However, Peumans says LED use cannot be considered in isolation from the wider lighting design. Large screens can produce significant amounts of light, potentially affecting the atmosphere of a space if they are not carefully integrated with other elements.

“Everything from us comes from light; we come from a theatrical background. But LED screens are also light,” he says. “The challenge will be to combine these tools—to create the right atmosphere using light combined with the LED screens or with content projection.”

This thinking also influences how Painting with Light approaches technology in the visitor experience. Rather than making the technology itself the focus, Peumans believes it should support the story and remain largely invisible to the audience.

“You always have to put technology behind the purpose of the story and not the other way around,” he says.

“In the end, maybe the audience doesn't really notice it. They should not notice it. That’s the good thing about technology; if they don't notice it, then it works.”

​Introducing IllumiSphere


This philosophy drove IllumiSphere's development. This new product moves beyond conventional flat-panel digital signage, using spinning LED technology to create the appearance of floating 3D animations visible from 360 degrees.


For Peter van Bilsen, commercial lead for Illumiware, the product’s development stemmed from a gap he identified through his work with operators.

Van Bilsen, who has spent years consulting with operators on hardware and design integration, saw destinations seeking high-impact visual experiences that could fit existing budgets and spaces.

IllumiSphere's core differentiator is its three-dimensional presence.

Traditional screens are linear, flat, and highly directional; guests must stand in front of them to experience the content. IllumiSphere uses spinning holographic LED technology encased in a durable, clear protective housing.

This creates the appearance of a floating, three-dimensional light sculpture that can be viewed from different angles.

Available in three sizes, from 230 mm to 400 mm, the units are designed for applications ranging from retail displays and indoor theming to outdoor plazas and queue lines.

Designed for commercial environments, the units feature an anti-UV polycarbonate shell and are rated IP65 for water and dust resistance and IK08 for impact protection. OSRAM LEDs provide up to 25,000 hours of operating life, supporting long-term use in high-traffic venues.

​Ease of deployment


While the technology is designed to create a sophisticated visual effect, it is intended to be straightforward to operate. Advanced AV systems can require specialist technicians, programming and control equipment, creating an additional operational consideration for attractions.

"Ease of deployment was central to our design," explains Van Bilsen. "It is so easy; it’s plug and play, so it doesn't need any special skills.”

Each IllumiSphere is self-contained, with 8GB of internal storage for MP4 content. Operators can upload new animations wirelessly via Wi-Fi, without accessing the hardware or connecting physical cables.


An online tool helps users format content for the spherical display, while a secure transmission dongle allows teams to update individual or multiple units at once. This gives operators a straightforward way to change campaigns, animations or seasonal content without physically modifying the installation.

Illumiware also provides pre-designed content alongside its hardware, recognising that not every attraction has an in-house team to create 3D animations.

Painting with Light has developed themed content packs for seasonal events, with each pack containing 10 looping video animations designed specifically for the IllumiSphere. The content uses high-contrast visuals against black backgrounds to enhance the holographic effect.

Six packs are currently available, covering Christmas, winter, Valentine’s Day, Easter, summer and Halloween. Operators can organise the animations into seasonal playlists and switch between them as required.

“We prepare a lot of content in advance, making a playlist for each season,” adds Van Bilsen. “And they only have to click on it, so it plays a different configuration.”

​Scaling up


Individual IllumiSpheres can be used for signage and smaller thematic elements, while multiple units can be combined into larger installations. One example is the IllumiTree, a 3.5-metre structure designed for public spaces, plazas and attraction entrances.

The standard IllumiTree incorporates 16 IllumiSpheres, although larger configurations can accommodate up to 32. The outdoor-rated structure uses low-voltage power and is designed for use in busy public environments.


Its digital content can be changed to suit different seasons, events or campaigns, allowing the physical structure to remain in place.

An IllumiTree can therefore take on different roles throughout the year, from a Christmas installation to an Easter feature or branded display, using the same underlying hardware.

​Beyond attractions


The IllumiSphere is designed for a range of environments, from attraction entrances and plazas to queue lines, dark rides, zoos and aquariums.

Its relatively small footprint and changeable content allow it to be used for theming, wayfinding or seasonal displays without permanent changes to the surrounding environment.

Queue lines are one potential application, providing a way to introduce visual content and storytelling into spaces that can otherwise be difficult to theme. Zoos and aquariums could also use the spheres for evening events, while theme parks and dark rides could incorporate them into existing scenic environments.


Illumiware is also targeting markets beyond traditional attractions, including hospitality and retail. Seasonal displays are one area of interest, while hotels and holiday accommodation could use the technology to add changing visual elements to lobbies and other shared spaces.

“We are indeed talking to companies in retail, especially because seasonal events are very important to them,” says Van Bilsen.

This wider application reflects the IllumiSphere’s focus on flexible digital content rather than a single attraction format.

​Reducing the operational burden


For operators, IllumiSphere's appeal goes beyond its visual impact. By shifting seasonal changes from physical decoration to digital content, the system could reduce some of the labour, storage, and logistical demands of repeated changeovers.

Traditional seasonal displays can require teams to install and dismantle decorations, store them between events and work at height in large spaces. A digital installation remains in place, with the visual treatment changed through its content.


“You hang them one time, and they hang the whole year,” says Van Bilsen. “It really gives them something where they say, ‘Oh yeah, let’s put on now the Easter content’—click, and it’s ready.”

The approach can also reduce the need to store large quantities of seasonal props and potentially extend the useful life of the physical installation.

For venues running multiple seasonal events, this could make it easier to refresh an environment without repeating the same physical changeover process several times a year.

​Rental opens the door


Illumiware has partnered with Blue-I Group to establish a rental and distribution route for the technology. Blue-I will be Illumiware’s exclusive rental partner in Europe, as well as its rental and sales partner in the UK and Ireland.

The IllumiSphere adds another visual technology to Blue-I's AV offering, with applications spanning seasonal displays, signage, exhibitions, brand activations and events.


“The purpose is to explore unique and creative technologies that can help agencies, designers and artists turn their ideas into practical, visually engaging solutions,” says Yves Melis of Blue-I Group.

“When we first saw IllumiSphere, we immediately recognised both its creative potential and its practical value.”

The rental model is particularly suited to temporary installations, including events, pop-ups and product launches. The spheres are designed to be lightweight and straightforward to install, with content prepared in advance for each project.

For organisations considering new technology, rental lets them test the IllumiSphere in a live environment before committing to a permanent installation.

“It is very much a case of ‘try before you buy’,” says Melis.

The approach also allows users to experiment with different configurations and content before committing to a permanent installation.

​Looking ahead


Illumiware will make its global debut at IAAPA Expo Europe in London, where Painting with Light is planning an immersive booth centred on the IllumiTree. The showcase will allow visitors to see the technology in a live environment.

For Luc Peumans, the launch also marks the next step in an idea that began during the COVID-19 pandemic: making some of the tools developed for Painting with Light’s bespoke projects available as products that other organisations can use.

“Why don't we make it available for other people to use? That’s the philosophy of this Illumiware brand,” he says.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by PWL - Painting With Light (@pwl_be)

The company is now looking at how the technology could develop alongside advances in real-time content and AI. Peumans sees potential for digital environments to become more responsive, with content adapting to visitors or changing in real time.

“Also, I'm really interested in what AI will bring,” he says. “The combination of all these things to create unique experiences in real time, adapted to a group of people, gives you a lot of opportunities.”

For Van Bilsen, the longer-term ambition is to move beyond individual installations and explore networks of connected IllumiSpheres across larger environments, including plazas, themed areas and event spaces.

The immediate focus, however, is on establishing the platform and demonstrating where it can add value. For attractions and other venues, the proposition is ultimately about changing the experience without having to change the physical environment around it.

Attendees at IAAPA Expo Europe 2026 in London, held from 22 – 24 September, can meet the Painting with Light team and discover IllumiSphere for themselves at booth #S4230.

title: Why LLMs are the new gatekeepers, and what it means for B2B discovery in the attractions industry
summary:
When The Observer covered global advertising giant WPP’s strategy, CEO Cindy Rose highlighted how rapidly commercial discovery is shifting.

Speaking on her role leading the company through this transition, she said: “Marketing and advertising is probably being transformed faster than almost any other industry.”

At the heart of that transformation is a fundamental reality captured by Nick Louisson, her director of commercial partnerships and agency services: "LLMs are essentially a new consumer."

As Louisson points out, brands must now appear in large language models (LLMs) to reach their audiences as search habits evolve. But unlike traditional Google search—where businesses could buy sponsored ads or bid their way to top rankings—most LLMs prioritise earned media derived from trusted legacy outlets.

Smartphones changed how visitors find and interact with attractions, and agentic AI is the next chapter

“Search has been dominated by Google, which was about understanding how to win with its algorithm, then – failing that – about buying your way to the top,” Louisson said.

“Now you must learn how to win with ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity. Currently, you must earn that performance; you can’t simply buy it.”

This shift is actively reshaping B2B decision-making across the attractions and leisure sectors.

Whether a museum director is looking for digital exhibit technology, a theme park developer is shortlisting ride manufacturers, or a resort operator is sourcing sustainable water park solutions, buyers are increasingly starting their research in conversation with AI.

They ask ChatGPT, Gemini, or Google AI Overviews to compare options, evaluate suppliers, and present a curated shortlist.

The scale of the market shift

The speed of this transition is reflected in recent research on commercial adoption. According to a landmark study by Forrester, an overwhelming 94% of B2B buyers now use AI to research vendors and evaluate options as part of their purchasing decisions.

As Forbes recently highlighted in an analysis on generative engine optimisation (GEO), the financial stakes of missing this layer are substantial. Roughly half of major search interactions now surface AI-generated summaries ahead of traditional results, a share that is rising fast.

When a brand is omitted from that first answer layer, it risks losing credibility by absence alone, effectively redirecting high-value commercial inquiries to competitors named as the default options.

Visibility no longer relies on sitting somewhere in a long list of search links; it depends entirely on being cited and trusted by the AI engine itself.

The travel sector: from ten links to a shortlist of three

The travel and tourism industry offers a clear view of where discovery is heading.

Research from leading travel site Skift highlights a stark reality for destination and supplier discovery: traditional search engines present ten blue links, but AI conversational tools condense that pool of choices down to a tight shortlist of just three recommendations.

AI Narrows Hotel Search to 3 Results and Changes Who Wins

Travel is a closely related sector, so this "winner-takes-all" curation similarly impacts attractions B2B suppliers.

When an operator prompts an AI for recommendations, the system extracts data from a handful of primary, trusted sources. If a business isn't embedded within those underlying sources, it is cut from the shortlist entirely.

How AI models decide who to trust

AI engines do not generate authority in a vacuum; they crawl, index, and learn from platforms that maintain high domain trust, structured data, and active human engagement.

For example, blooloop is already the most-read media resource in the visitor attractions sector, but our reach also extends far beyond human readership: our domain trust ensures we rank alongside major global news publishers in AI search visibility.

In a recent global media study of over 15 million AI responses by Muck Rack, blooloop ranked in the UK Top 10 for AI visibility alongside mainstream news outlets like The Guardian and the Financial Times. Additionally, news editor Bea Mitchell was named the #4 most-cited journalist globally by AI engines.

Our AI ongoing strategy

blooloop has a Domain Authority of 75 built on decades of delivering trusted content to visitor attraction professionals. When an LLM delivers industry news or supplier information across attraction design, technology, or operations, it leans on us as a high-trust, human-validated network to form its answers.

blooloop has boosted its AI visibility with eight new regional websites

To supercharge this AI visibility globally and future-proof coverage across key growth regions, we have recently expanded our digital infrastructure beyond a single .com domain.

The launch of our 8 new regional websites across key global markets, from China and the Middle East to Latin America, serves a double structural role:

  • Delivering localised, native-language news to real human decision-makers on the ground.
  • Supplying geographically relevant entity data directly to AI search crawlers worldwide.

Do feed the algorithms

Navigating the next era of discovery isn't an either/or choice between human audiences and machine algorithms. The primary driver of AI trust remains genuine human readership and rigorous editorial standards maintained over years.

A great company website is perfect for converting visitors who already know you, but it won't get you surfaced by AI search engines in the first place.

To be recommended by LLMs as buyers research their options, your brand must now be embedded in the trusted, established media sources that feed those algorithms.

title: Zamperla unveils captivating new attraction, Hypnosiz
summary:
Zamperla, a leading ride manufacturer, has premiered its latest attraction, Hypnosiz, as part of its 60th-anniversary celebrations at the company’s headquarters in Altavilla Vicentina, Italy.

After six decades of designing and manufacturing rides, Zamperla marked its anniversary by presenting a new attraction designed to serve as a visual landmark within the park and deliver a standout experience for guests.

The unveiling followed a tour of the company's facilities, which gave an international delegation of clients, partners, media, and industry professionals insight into the engineering, manufacturing, creativity, and expertise that drive Zamperla’s attractions.

Evolving Nebulaz

Hypnosiz is the next evolution of the iconic Zamperla bestseller, Nebulaz. The new ride retains the original's distinctive hypnotic movement and its capacity to create interaction between guests, while pushing the concept further with increased capacity, greater scale, a stronger visual presence, and elevated landmark appeal.

Antonio Zamperla, president and CEO of Zamperla, says: "Nebulaz has been a very successful product for us, but what I have always liked about it is that you don’t necessarily have to ride it to enjoy it. You can stand twenty meters away, look at it moving, and still wonder how the gondolas do not hit each other.

"There is something almost hypnotic about that movement.

"With Hypnosiz, we wanted to keep that DNA: the recognizable movement and the interaction between riders, but take it much further. We wanted something bigger, with more capacity, more presence, and much more visual impact."

The design of Hypnosiz seeks to foster a shared, fun experienceImage courtesy of Zamperla

Hypnosiz reaches 11.4 metres tall and has a 16-metre footprint. The ride accommodates 64 adults, with a maximum theoretical hourly capacity of 650 passengers.

Elegant engineering

Hypnosiz' development was shaped by a central engineering requirement to create a larger, more engaging experience that would streamline the machine’s operation and maintenance.

This demonstrates Zamperla’s approach to innovation, which is not necessarily about adding technology. Rather, the most intelligent solution is sometimes identifying what can be removed while maintaining or enhancing the experience.

A highlight of Hypnosiz is its seat arrangement, with visitors facing one another. As the ride moves, the experience becomes more social and shared. Riders can see the reactions of those around them, and laughter, excitement, and screams become an integral part of the ride.

Hypnosiz features an engaging design that is fun to both ride and watchImage courtesy of Zamperla

The new product is designed not only to entertain its riders, but also to engage its spectators. The attraction becomes the visual centrepiece of its surroundings, using movement, scale, and lighting to create a strong visual presence that is particularly captivating at night.

"A good attraction should entertain the people on board," says Zamperla, "but a great attraction can also change the energy of the space around it."

Earlier this year, Zamperla provided three rides to Idefix’ Abenteuerland, a new immersive themed area at Belantis in Germany, inspired by the world of Asterix & Obelix.

title: Disney World to beta test AI-powered vacation booking tool
summary:
Walt Disney World in Florida is preparing to beta test a new AI-powered booking experience designed to help guests plan their Disney vacations.

Developed with Google Cloud, the new tool will allow selected users to ask booking questions conversationally, compare pricing and availability, and receive personalised recommendations.

Instead of searching through Disney’s website for the right hotel, guests will be able to tell the AI what matters most to them, from their favourite Disney characters to easy access to a particular theme park.

Walt Disney World in Florida is preparing to beta test a new AI-powered booking experienceDisney

For example, a user could share that they are visiting Magic Kingdom with their family for their son's 7th birthday, who is a fan of The Lion King.

They could provide context via a natural-language input, such as "easy access to the parks, a nice pool, and any available offers".

Disney will then provide AI-generated summaries with information on rates and availability, as well as personalised suggestions.

To begin with, the beta test will roll out to selected users in the US and Canada, with Disney planning a wider phased launch based on guest feedback.

As above, Disney has partnered with Google Cloud for the AI elements of the new vacation booking engine, which will take information from official Disney data rather than the whole internet.

Disney adds AI to trip planning

“We’re partnering with Google Cloud on the AI portion of this, but we are using Disney sources and data underpinning that,” a Disney representative said during a media briefing, via CNET.

Disney is already using AI to design, build and operate its parks and experiences, including AI-powered digital twins and simulation tools to design and test new attractions.

The company has also made its J.A.R.V.I.S. AI tool available to more than 2,000 Disney Imagineers.

Alongside its most recent earnings, Disney said it views emerging technologies like AI as "a significant opportunity for our company to drive returns".

title: ​Severn Lamb and the changing face of attraction transport
summary:
Known for its heritage trains and trackless road trams, Severn Lamb is expanding its electric vehicle portfolio to meet the wider mobility needs of visitor attractions.

The Warwickshire-based manufacturer has traditionally focused on guest transport, with tracked trains, trams and road trains used across theme parks, resorts and other destinations. It is now broadening its offer to include compact electric vehicles for behind-the-scenes operations, from maintenance and security to housekeeping and logistics.

As attractions become larger and more complex, operators need mobility solutions that support both the visitor experience and the day-to-day running of the site. Severn Lamb's expanded EV portfolio is designed to address both.

Blooloop speaks to Patrick Lamb, managing director of Severn Lamb, about the changing mobility needs of visitor attractions and the role of electric vehicles in supporting guest and back-of-house operations.

​Beyond the guest journey


Electric propulsion is not new to Severn Lamb, explains Lamb. “We have been developing battery-electric passenger transport solutions for many years. What has changed is the breadth of the requirements we are being asked to meet.”


Severn Lamb's customers increasingly need more than vehicles for transporting large groups of visitors. They also need smaller vehicles for accessible transport, staff movement, maintenance, security, landscaping and other site operations.

“Expanding our portfolio allows us to support that complete mobility picture, from compact passenger and utility vehicles through to higher-capacity shuttles, road trams and rail systems."

"It is a natural extension of what Severn Lamb has always done: understanding how people and equipment need to move around a destination and providing the most appropriate solution.”

​The invisible network behind the visitor experience


When discussing transport at visitor attractions, the focus tends to be on the highly visible elements: the entrance tram, the themed train circling a safari park or the scenic monorail. Behind these systems, however, is a continuous network of back-of-house logistics.

This behind-the-scenes movement of people, equipment, supplies and waste is vital to keeping a site running. Problems within this network can ultimately affect the guest experience.

"Visitors may never see most of the work taking place behind the scenes, but their experience depends upon it being carried out efficiently,” says Lamb.

“Maintenance teams need to respond quickly, catering and retail supplies must reach the right locations, waste has to be removed, landscapes and facilities must be maintained, and security staff need to move around the site effectively.

"At zoos, there may also be equipment and supplies required for animal care.”


An appropriate back-of-house fleet can therefore improve productivity while also helping a site remain clean, safe and welcoming.

“It is an essential part of the overall guest experience, even if it is rarely visible."

Traditionally, attractions relied on conventional vehicles to handle these tasks. However, a conventional van or larger utility vehicle driving through a tranquil botanical garden or near sensitive animal enclosures can break the immersion that theme parks and heritage attractions work to maintain.

"We are seeing growing interest from operators who want to replace conventional vehicles with something cleaner, quieter and better suited to the environment in which they are working," says Lamb.

"Many attractions operate across large or complex sites, but the majority of their daily journeys are relatively short and predictable. Staff may be transporting tools, supplies, waste or small groups of people throughout the day, often using vehicles that are larger than the task requires.”

Compact electric vehicles are well suited to this type of work.

"They are easy to manoeuvre, can be configured for different operational roles and can return to a central location for charging. Sustainability targets may begin the conversation, but efficiency, practicality and operating costs are increasingly important factors too."

​Expanding the electric fleet


Partnerships with WAEV Inc. and EVX Mobility support Severn Lamb's expanded EV offering.

Announced in June 2026, Severn Lamb's partnership with WAEV Inc. brings WAEV's Compact Mobility and Utility EV ranges into its portfolio. US-based WAEV offers light-duty electric vehicles supported by a network of dealers and service centres.

The partnership also gives Severn Lamb access to WAEV's dealer and service network.

The partnership with EVX Mobility adds passenger-focused electric vehicles to complement the WAEV utility and compact range, including the Solar Shuttle.

"The continued development of our electric vehicle offering marks an important step for Severn Lamb," says Lamb.

"By building on our partnership with EVX and introducing WAEV's Compact Mobility and Utility EV ranges, we are expanding the range of sustainable solutions available to our customers and strengthening our ability to support a wider variety of operational needs."


WAEV's product line offers durable utility electric vehicles built for demanding site operations. Models including the Bigfoot, GEM eL XD and Fusion Utility are designed for applications including maintenance, landscaping, logistics and site support.

"The greatest value is generally found in frequent, repeatable journeys where a conventional van or larger utility vehicle would be inefficient or intrusive," Patrick Lamb says.

"Utility EVs can transport tools, maintenance equipment, landscaping materials, deliveries and waste around a site. Compact passenger vehicles can support security patrols, staff movement, inspections and the transport of guests who require additional assistance."

For example, utility vehicles can be configured to carry maintenance equipment, landscaping materials and other bulky loads. They can also support catering, retail restocking and waste collection, particularly where staff and visitors share routes.

Their smaller footprint can be useful at attractions where staff and visitors share routes, reducing the physical presence of service vehicles.

"Different configurations allow operators to choose a vehicle suited to the task rather than adapting their operation around a standard vehicle," Lamb explains.

​Supporting the guest journey


Alongside its utility vehicles, Severn Lamb's expanded portfolio includes compact passenger vehicles for resorts, gardens, historic sites and campuses.

The portfolio includes the GEM e2, e4 and e6, the wheelchair-accessible GEM WAV, GEM Ambulance, ShuttlePro XL and Fusion Passenger. Applications include guest and VIP transport, staff journeys and security, while the GEM Ambulance is designed for medical response teams operating on busy sites.

Accessibility is another important factor to consider, with features including wheelchair ramps, flexible seating and space for mobility equipment.


"Accessibility increasingly needs to be considered from the beginning of a transport project rather than added later," says Lamb.

"Attractions serve guests with a wide range of mobility requirements, including wheelchair users, older visitors and people who may find it difficult to cover long distances.

“The wider fleet also needs to provide enough flexibility to support individual journeys as well as larger-group transport. Good accessible transport should feel like an integrated part of the visitor experience, not a separate or secondary service.”

For higher-capacity routes, Severn Lamb also offers the EVX-powered Solar Shuttle.

"The Solar Shuttle bridges the gap between compact passenger vehicles and our larger road tram and rail solutions. With configurations for approximately 11 to 24 passengers, it is suited to regular routes around attractions, resorts, gardens, campuses and heritage destinations.”

The Solar Shuttle features a solar-assisted roof, wheelchair access and fleet-management capabilities.

​Planning for real-world conditions


For visitor attraction operators, electrifying a fleet requires more than replacing petrol or diesel vehicles with electric equivalents. Operators need to understand how vehicles will be used day to day, from mileage and payload to terrain, operating hours, and seasonal demand.

Lamb says the process should start with the task, not the technology: "Operators need to understand actual daily mileage, payload, passenger numbers, gradients, road surfaces, operating hours and seasonal peaks.

“The vehicle must provide sufficient real-world range with an appropriate margin, while charging needs to fit naturally into the operating schedule. Payload and towing capacity should be assessed carefully, because an unsuitable vehicle will create inefficiency regardless of its power source."


Key considerations include the vehicle's duty cycle, terrain, climate and charging requirements. Attractions may also need to account for gradients, gravel or cobbled surfaces, weather conditions and charging requirements. Charging can be scheduled around operating patterns, whether overnight at a depot or during planned breaks.

Seasonal peaks are another important consideration. Designing a fleet around an average operating day can leave operators short of capacity when visitor numbers are highest.

"One of the clearest lessons is that the operating environment is often more complex than it initially appears.

"The busiest day of the year, rather than an average day, can reveal what a transport system really needs to deliver. Route conditions, gradients, weather, accessibility, charging opportunities and maintenance support can all influence the correct solution.

“We are also seeing greater interest in flexible layouts and fleet-management technology, as operators want better visibility of how their vehicles are being used. These conversations reinforce the importance of listening before proposing a product.”

​Making the business case


While sustainability targets may prompt fleet electrification, operators also need a clear commercial case for investing in electric vehicles. That means looking beyond the purchase price to total cost of ownership, including energy, servicing, downtime and residual value.

"The strongest business case is often found in vehicles completing frequent, predictable journeys and returning regularly to a central base," explains Lamb. "This makes charging easier to plan and allows operators to make full use of the vehicle throughout its working life.”

Beyond reducing tailpipe emissions, electric vehicles can offer lower energy costs, reduced routine maintenance and quieter operation. Quieter operation is particularly valuable in visitor areas, around animals and near hotels or accommodation.


The business case should therefore consider the vehicle's full operating life, including purchase cost, energy, servicing, downtime and residual value.

"Space is extremely valuable at most attractions," says Lamb.

"Routes may be narrow, shared with pedestrians or constrained by existing buildings, landscaping and historic infrastructure. A compact EV can negotiate tighter spaces, require less parking and operate with less disruption than a conventional road vehicle.

“This is particularly useful at heritage sites, gardens and established attractions where routes cannot easily be widened or altered.

​Towards more connected fleets


As attractions move towards lower-emission operations, site fleets are likely to become more electric, connected and tailored to specific tasks.

Rather than relying on one vehicle type, operators can combine compact passenger vehicles, utility vehicles, shuttles, and larger transport systems to meet the needs of different routes and tasks.

Lamb expects this shift to accelerate over the next five to 10 years, with data and smart technology playing a growing role.

"Attraction fleets will become increasingly electric, connected and task-specific. Rather than using one type of vehicle for every purpose, operators will build integrated fleets in which compact passenger vehicles, utility platforms, shuttles and larger transport systems each perform the work for which they are best suited.

“We are also likely to see greater use of fleet data, smarter charging and more emphasis on accessibility, whole-life costs and service support. The transition will not happen at the same speed everywhere, but the overall direction is clear."


Fleet-management systems and telematics can give operators greater visibility into vehicle location, battery performance, and maintenance needs, while smarter charging can help them manage energy use and costs.

The expansion of electric vehicles reflects a broader shift in how attractions approach site mobility. Electric vehicles can increasingly support both guest-facing transport and the back-of-house operations that keep attractions running.

For operators, the challenge is likely to be less about choosing between electric and conventional vehicles and more about determining where different types of electric vehicles can deliver the greatest operational value.

As fleets become more specialised, the emphasis will be on matching vehicles to the realities of each site, from guest transport and accessibility to maintenance, logistics and other back-of-house needs.

"Severn Lamb wants to be a long-term mobility partner within that transition, combining our established experience in passenger transport with a much broader electric vehicle portfolio,” concludes Lamb.

“Our aim is to help operators select the right solution for every part of their site, from behind-the-scenes operations to the guest journey."

Meet the Severn Lamb team in London at IAAPA Expo Europe 2026 from 22 – 24 September at booth #S1416 and in Orlando at IAAPA Expo 2026 from 17 – 20 November at booth #S3728 and #S3832.
